one_liner: Header-only C++ big-number types; fixed-width cpp_int (128-bit) beats GMP's mpz on basic arithmetic by 1.5-6x.
what_it_does: Boost.Multiprecision wraps big integers, rationals and floats in a generic number<> front end with pluggable backends (its own header-only cpp_int/cpp_bin_float/cpp_dec_float, or GMP, MPFR, MPIR, TomMath). cpp_int_backend<MinBits, MaxBits, SignType, Checked, Allocator> gives either an arbitrary-precision heap type or, with MinBits == MaxBits and Allocator void, a fixed-width stack type such as int128_t/int256_t/uint1024_t. All types behave like built-in integers with operators and interoperate with Boost.Math.
how_it_is_fast: Fixed-width cpp_int stores its limbs inline with no heap allocation and no runtime size checks beyond the fixed limb count, so small-width operations avoid the allocation and dispatch overhead GMP's mpz layer pays per call. Expression templates (enabled by default) fuse compound expressions and cut temporaries. Fixed-precision types are also constexpr-capable, so constant arithmetic can be folded at compile time.
when_to_use: 128-bit integer arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %, xor) in hot loops, where the docs measure fixed cpp_int 1.5-5.9x faster than gmp_int
256-bit-ish workloads dominated by add/sub/construct or many temporaries (Voronoi builder test: int256_t 3.8x faster than mpz_int)
Projects that need a permissively licensed (BSL-1.0), header-only bigint with no GMP/LGPL dependency
Compile-time (constexpr) big-integer constants with fixed-width types
Code that wants one generic interface and may swap to the GMP backend later
when_not_to_use: Multiplication, division or modulus at 256 bits and above: gmp_int wins (256-bit * 1.77x, / 1.72x slower for fixed cpp_int; 512/1024-bit * ~1.5-1.6x slower)
Modular exponentiation / primality testing on wide types: Miller-Rabin with uint1024_t and cpp_int runs ~9-11x slower than mpz_int
Dynamic (arbitrary-precision) cpp_int in general: it is slower than GMP at every size in the integer_performance tables
Very large numbers (thousands of bits and up) where GMP/FLINT's subquadratic algorithms matter

integration.dependencies: Boost.Config only in standalone mode (BOOST_MP_STANDALONE); otherwise other Boost headers; optional GMP/MPFR/MPIR/TomMath for those backends
integration.min_toolchain: C++14; constexpr cpp_int arithmetic needs C++2a or GCC 6+ in C++14 mode
integration.platforms: any platform with a compliant C++14 compiler
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same number<> interface can host gmp_int or cpp_int, so switching mpz_int to a fixed cpp_int is a typedef change, but it is not a drop-in for raw mpz_t C code

gotchas: Fixed-width types use sign-magnitude, not two's complement: int128_t has 128 magnitude bits plus a sign bit and is one machine word larger than expected
Unchecked fixed types wrap modulo 2^MaxBits silently; checked_* variants throw std::overflow_error instead
Division by zero throws std::overflow_error; negative values cannot be printed in hex or octal
Disabling expression templates can cost a lot (Miller-Rabin: cpp_int 16.2x vs 11.2x of GMP's time without/with them)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over ctbignum or mp++ when you want a mature Boost-licensed header-only type with full operator coverage, signed types and Boost.Math interop rather than maximum small-limb speed; pick FLINT or mp++ for large operands and number-theory kernels where GMP-class algorithms dominate.
verified_claims_summary: Boost's own docs (GCC 10.3.0, GMP 6.2.0, Boost 1.78, run 2021-09-30; CPU and flags not stated) time 500,000 ops excluding allocation/copy: fixed 128-bit cpp_int beats gmp_int on * (4.80x), + (5.87x), / (1.70x), % (1.47x); at 256 bits it still wins + (1.45x) but loses *, / and %, and GMP wins all 512/1024-bit multiply and modulus rows.
status_note: Actively maintained Boost library (commits through Sept 2026), BSL-1.0 and header-only, so it is easy to vendor; the published performance tables are from 2021 and may not reflect current versions.
